title: Molecular Mechanisms Regulating Uterus Development
text:
The uterus contains glands that are essential for pregnancy and contribute to uterine-based endometrial disorders and
disease, yet the developmental biology of epithelium and gland differentiation remains poorly understood. This gap in our
knowledge will be addressed through an integrative systems biology approach that will define critical cellular and molecular
pathways governing epithelial differentiation and gland development in the newborn uterus. This research is expected to
significantly advance our understanding of the developmental aspects of uterine biology, determinants of adult uterine
function, and provide a foundation for the design of clinical therapies to prevent, identify and treat human reproductive
problems involving uterine dysgenesis, dysplasia, or dysfunction.

title: Immunobiology Program
text: Project Summary – Immunobiology Program The Immunobiology Program (IMB) serves as a rich resource for the Abramson Cancer Center (ACC) in advancing an understanding of immunobiology and immunotherapy of cancer. The Program aims to: 1) Understand the fundamental aspects of immune biology, including leukocyte activation, differentiation, inactivation, and transformation as these relate to cancer; 2) Forge a comprehensive understanding of tumor immune surveillance using state-of-the art in vitro, animal model, and human experimental systems; and 3) Guide translation of novel clinical strategies for immunotherapy of cancer by leading or collaborating on human clinical trials. Established in 1974, this Research Program received “Exceptional” merit at the time of the last CCSG renewal application. The Program co-Leaders (PLs) are Warren Pear, MD, PhD, an expert in the molecular biology of leukocyte development and malignant transformation and E. John Wherry, PhD, a leader in tumor immunology, immune exhaustion and immunotherapy. Drs. Pear and Wherry are experienced, NCI- funded investigators who are highly collaborative and whose research interests span the realm of basic and translational science. There are 39 Program members from nine departments and three schools with long- standing intra- and inter-Programmatic collaborations spanning the basic, clinical, and population science Programs. Members include international leaders in basic immunology, tumor immunobiology and translational immunotherapy who have driven landmark breakthroughs such as molecularly defining T cell exhaustion, dissecting the biologic response to checkpoint inhibition, and developing CAR T cells that revolutionized cellular therapy for cancer. IMB collaborates extensively with other Programs for clinical translation and biomarker discovery. For example, CART19 T cells were designed in IMB then translated to the clinic with members of the Hematologic Malignancies and Pediatric Oncology Programs in studies that led to two FDA- approved indications. The PLs facilitate interactions through multiple weekly seminars and meetings, promotion of collaborative grants and projects, two annual research retreats, pilot project grants, and training programs. During the current project period, PLs recruited 11 new Full members, expanded important forums, facilitated new collaborative grants, initiated new ACC-wide initiatives, and were actively involved in decisions regarding new and existing Shared Resources. Currently, Program members have $24.2M in research grant funding (annual direct costs), of which $15.1M is peer-reviewed and $4.1M is NCI-funded. The Program holds 38 R01-equivalents. During the current project period, Program members published 468 cancer-related publications, many of which are in top journals in the field. Of these, 19% are intra-Programmatic, 32% are inter-Programmatic, and 72% are multi-institutional.

title: Investigating the Role of B-cells in Durable Complete Responses to Immunotherapy in Head and Neck Cancer
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because of its focus on the mechanisms underlying
complete, durable responses to immunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), and the
antitumor activity of B cells and B-cell mediated antibodies. A greater understanding of the role of B cells in
exceptional responses to immunotherapy will provide insight into anti-tumor immunity that can be exploited to
improve immunotherapeutic approaches and increase complete response rates. Ultimately the proposed
research will improve understanding of the mechanisms involved in the progression and response to treatment
in HNSCC and is thus relevant to the NCI's mission of supporting cancer research that advances scientific
knowledge and helps people live longer, healthier lives.

title: Population genetics of human evolutionary history and natural selection
text:
Human population dynamics and evolutionary history have combined to shape the genomes of people living
today, impacting human health, disease susceptibility and our understanding of broader societal and historical
questions. We learn about evolutionary processes by studying genetic variation among sequenced individuals,
analyses which are grounded in mathematical and statistical innovations. This research will integrate
mathematical and empirical approaches to learn key features of our species’ evolutionary history and how that
history shapes genetic and phenotypic variation across populations.

title: Investigating Thalamocortical Spike Dynamics to Increase Sleep Stability and Memory in Alzheimer’s Disease
text:
Sleep fragmentation is associated with Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and other dementias from early stages and
contributes to disease worsening and memory decline. Our goal is twofold: 1) to discover cellular mechanisms
that promote sleep stability and 2) to leverage sleep mechanisms to delay AD progression and memory decline
in a rat model of Alzheimer’s Disease. The results will help develop novel treatments for AD based on improving
sleep function.

title: Childhood Hematological Malignancies Training Program
text: This program enhances research training for young scientists to promote the next generation of independent investigators studying childhood blood cancers. Advanced approaches in genomic analysis, experimental modeling, and translational research will be integrated to enhance training for scientists early in their research careers. The long-term goal is to improve the understanding and treatment of childhood blood and lymph cancers by advancing research progress in this field.

title: Training in Translational Science and Cardiovascular Research
text:
This is a research training program for postdoctoral fellows at Oregon Health & Science
University, Portland, Oregon. The proposed program will address an urgent need for
cardiovascular scientists who are trained broadly in translational sciences focused on
cardiovascular disease. The program will train 30 scientists who will join the ranks of academia
and promote cutting-edge research in heart disease.

title: Role of GLIS3 in Human Pancreatic Beta Cell Generation, Survival and Proliferation
text:
Narrative.
Although genome-wide association studies have identified numerous genes and variants associated with
diabetes, the exact biological functions of these genes/variants in human pancreatic β cells are largely
unknown. Here, we will use human embryonic stem cells, human islets, and humanized mice to systematically
study the role of these genetic variants in human pancreatic β cell development, function, and survival in vitro
and in vivo. Understanding the biological functions of these genes/variants will significantly enhance our
knowledge of β cell biology, which will pave the way for the development of drugs for precision therapy for
diabetes patients.

title: The role of long noncoding RNA CRNDE in normal physiology and cancer
text:
This research proposes to investigate how long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), a diverse class of RNAs with
poorly understood functions, contribute to the pathogenesis of cancer, a leading cause of death in the United
States. In particular, we will study the role of lncRNAs in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), a deadly malignancy with
limited effective treatment options. A better understanding of noncoding RNAs could enable the development
of new therapeutic strategies for cancer patients.

title: Signaling dynamics in orchestrating stem cell functions during mammalian tissue regeneration
text:
Our tissues rely on the teamwork of special cells called stem cells to stay healthy. The proposed research aims
to use novel approaches to understand how stem cells work together to regenerate tissue and maintain normal
tissue functions. The knowledge gained from this study will help us design novel strategies for treating diseases
through regenerative medicine.

title: Machine Learning Guided Precision Genetic Testing for Identification of Monogenic Cardiovascular Disorders
text:
In rare genetic heart disease, early identification of at-risk individuals is important so that disease may be
prevented or treated in the patient, but these diseases are often underdiagnosed. In this study, we will use
innovative artificial intelligence approaches on heart images and medical record data to identify patients who
may have evidence of an undiagnosed rare genetic heart disease, with a focus on hypertrophic
cardiomyopathy and transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. The results of this study could help create algorithms to
identify undiagnosed diseases in patients and help guide them towards treatments.

title: Directed Evolution of Novel AAVs and Regulatory Elements for Selective Microglial Gene Expression
text:
Microglial inflammation has been implicated in the pathology of numerous neurodegenerative
diseases, neurodevelopmental disorders, and other neurological conditions, and suppressing the
activation of innate immune signaling pathways in these cells could thus represent a broad
therapeutic approach. To enhance the efficacy and safety of such an approach, the intervention
should be both long-term and targeted to microglia, such that a gene therapy based on an adeno-
associated viral (AAV) vector would be promising. Since natural AAVs exhibit inefficient, non-targeted
delivery to human microglia, however, we propose to integrate directed evolution of AAV with
molecular barcoding, single cell next generation sequencing (NGS), machine learning, and human
tissue and non-human primate (NHP) brain models to develop AAVs for selective gene delivery of
potential therapeutic cargoes to primate microglia.

title: Targeting Declining DNA Repair in Oocyte Aging
text:
All females are affected by reproductive aging. Impaired DNA Repair is emerging as a key
mechanism in oocyte aging. The same mechanism appears to be shared with genetically driven cancer and
overall aging, severely impacting overall health. If the mechanisms behind age-induced decline in DNA repair
and oocyte aging are understood, targeted treatments can be developed to treat, retard, or prevent
reproductive senescence and improve reproductive and overall health.

title: Gene Editing and Silencing in Phototransduction
text:
Our new preclinical adRP model could also be useful for testing of future gene- and drug-based
therapies. The proposed research is innovative, as it introduces new methods and model
systems as the initial steps of a precision medicine approach toward developing adRP treatment.
These methods are also potentially adaptable to therapies based on targeting DNA sequences of
genes linked to other dominant disorders.

title: Regulation of single cell migration in vivo
text:
How do cells navigate through a complex environment? The ability of cells to move is critical for normal
development and often goes awry in disease. Thus, we propose to answer this question by directly visualizing,
and then manipulating, structures that cells make when they move in an intact living organism.

title: Genetics of early onset retinal diseases
text:
Description
The goal of this research project is to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms of human early onset
inherited retinal diseases, the most severe form of visual impairment. Through studying of the Tlcd3b mutant
mice model just established, we plan to reveal how changes in ceramide homeostasis leads to retinal
degeneration in human. In parallel, we propose to improve the rate of molecular diagnostic for the disease by
identifying novel pathogenic mutations and disease associated genes that will address a major gap of the field
and provide the basis for developing new therapy.

title: Mechanisms of Advanced NAFLD Disparities in Hispanics:  A Multi-level Analysis
text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common cause of chronic liver disease in modern society. NAFLD is predicted to become the leading indication for liver transplantation and is a risk factor for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma that can develop even without cirrhosis. In a large Hispanic and non-Hispanic White population with unequivocally staged levels of fibrosis, we will combine state-of-the-art approaches (e.g., lifestyle and environmental factors, genetic variation analyses, single-cell transcriptomic analyses of peripheral innate immune cells resulting in identification of diagnostic protein biomarkers, and structural integrated analyses) to gain novel mechanistic insights into NAFLD risk in Hispanics and disease progression to fibrosis which is the single most important predictor of outcome.

title: PyReconstruct2: Enhanced Modular, High-throughput, Interoperable, Connectomics Level Annotation Software
text:
Detailed maps of brain circuits at the nanometer scale are fundamental to understanding how the brain works,
but current methods are limited by a fragmented software landscape and the need for manual human
intervention. The goal of this project is to enhance PyReconstruct, a widely used platform for 3D
reconstruction, with infrastructure to handle 1000x larger reconstructions, and integrate state-of-the-art AI tools
as easy-to-use plugins. PyReconstruct2 will overcome current limitations and since it is freely available, it will
serve to democratize nanoscale research towards understanding normal circuit function and ultimately disease
processes.

title: Mechanism and approach to inactivate mutant KRAS of lung metastatic colon cancer by RNA-ligand-displaying exosome to co-deliver dCas9--gRNA ribonucleoprotein complex and KRAS siRNA
text:
Colon cancer is the second most common cause of cancer death primarily due to the undruggable mutations to
KRAS and subsequent lung metastasis with expected survival of only a few months. This proposal develops
approaches for inactivating mutant KRAS via RNA-ligand displaying exosomes loaded with dCas9-HDAC1-
gRNA ribonucleoprotein, siRNAs, and chemical drugs individually or in combination. The mechanisms of
silencing mutant KRAS genes will be investigated.

title: Regulation, function, and the therapeutic potential of an oncogenic long noncoding RNA lnc-HLX-2-7 in group 3 medulloblastomas
text:
Medulloblastoma requires aggressive therapy in all cases. It frequently recurs as resistance to
treatment and is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Also, affected individuals often
suffer from disorders secondary to therapy.
